chapter_title: Out in the Garden (Toys and Games)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Stepping into the Garden — First Read and Explore

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.41): answer three questions about ball-play, kite-play, and location.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud twice from the textbook (pp.39–40), pointing to each stanza. Students listen with books open and follow the text with their finger.
Shared read-aloud: the class reads the poem together with the teacher, one stanza at a time. The teacher pauses after each stanza to invite brief oral observations about the action words in it.
Let us think — A (p.41): students answer all three questions orally in pairs first, then write their answers independently in their exercise books. Teacher circulates and offers brief feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's three stanzas share an identical opening refrain; students often race past it — slow down to help them notice the repeated lines before moving into the action verbs. All three questions in the task are answered within the poem itself, so encourage children to look back at the text before writing.

periods.activity_title: Reading Deeper — Repeated Reading for Fluency

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.41): revisit and discuss all three comprehension questions as a class.

time_bands.activity: Quick paired chant: student pairs re-read the poem aloud together, switching who leads each stanza. Teacher listens for phrasing and energy rather than correcting individual words.
Whole-class review of Let us think — A (p.41): the teacher reads each question aloud, nominates different students to share their written answers, and builds a shared correct response on the board.
Unhurried guided reading: students re-read the poem independently and underline every action verb they find. Pairs compare their lists, and the class pools findings in a shared column on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem together in an earlier sitting, students arrive with some familiarity — use that to push toward fluency and word-level attention rather than re-explaining the story. Students sometimes miss 'tug' and 'sway' as action verbs; prompt them by miming the actions while saying the words.

periods.activity_title: Talk About Play — Guided Conversation and Picture Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.41): discuss where children play, outdoor games, and safety while playing.

time_bands.activity: Quick paired chant of the poem's action-verb lines ('I bounce my ball, I throw my ball…') with body actions. This warms up voice and movement before speaking tasks.

Let us think — B (p.41): teacher poses each question to the class one at a time, inviting at least three different students to respond. For question 3 (safety while playing), teacher models a complete sentence answer before students give their own.

Students share their responses in small groups of three; each group agrees on one safety rule and nominates a speaker to report it to the class. Teacher notes recurring ideas on the board without evaluating.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 3 — what happens if we are not careful — often produces single-word responses; ask follow-up prompts such as 'Can you say more about that?' to extend children into full sentences. Accept answers in any language and gently rephrase them in English as a model.

periods.activity_title: Traditional Games — Picture Talk and Mother-Tongue Bridge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.41): describe traditional games pictured, share names in mother tongue.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks students through the four illustrations on Textbook p.41 (tug-of-war, tin telephone, yo-yo, seven stones) one by one, naming each game and asking 'What do you see in this picture?'

Let us speak (p.41): in pairs, students choose one picture game they know, describe what players do in it, and share the game's name in their mother tongue. Each pair then reports to the class in two or three sentences in English.

Class discussion: teacher invites students to compare one game from the pictures with a game from the poem — what is similar, what is different? Students speak in turns; teacher helps shape their observations into full sentences on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Tug-of-war and seven stones are usually well-known, but the tin telephone may be unfamiliar; have a simple verbal description ready. Encouraging mother-tongue names shows students that their home language is a resource, not a barrier, and generates genuine enthusiasm for talking.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (pp.42–43): combine word pairs using 'and'; generate two original word pairs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem's third stanza aloud and highlights the paired lines: 'We run and skip / We jump and sway / We slide and swing.' Students repeat each pair twice and mime the actions as they say the words.

Let us learn (p.42): teacher models the pattern on the board with the example 'give and take', explaining how 'and' links two related words. Students complete the four fill-in items (sing–dance, eat–drink, catch–throw, run–catch) in their exercise books.

Let us learn (p.43): students think of two more word pairs of their own and write them using the same pattern. Pairs share their invented combinations with the class; teacher notes novel and creative examples on the board and prompts brief discussion of why the pairs feel natural together.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'and' connector links action-verb pairs in the poem's third stanza — pointing to those exact lines keeps the grammar grounded in the poem rather than feeling like an isolated drill. Some children may write word pairs that do not conventionally go together; treat these as creative exploration and redirect gently toward familiar pairings.

periods.activity_title: Paper Bag Puppet — Make, Decorate, Perform

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — Paper Bag Puppet (p.43): make a puppet following the nine-step process and use it to speak.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates steps 1–5 of the paper bag puppet process (Textbook p.43) slowly at the front, narrating each move aloud. Students watch with materials on their desks, not yet making.

Students follow steps 1–9 independently at their desks, using their own paper bags, colour pencils, woollen thread, and gum to create and decorate their puppet. Teacher circulates, assisting with the fold-and-draw steps.

Puppet show: students slide a hand into their finished puppet and take turns making the puppet 'say' one action from the poem — e.g. 'I bounce my ball!' Teacher encourages clear voices and playful delivery. Any remaining decoration time is used at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: Collect paper bags before the sitting so every student has one — the craft cannot start without the base material. The puppet performance naturally reinforces the poem's action verbs; nudge students toward the poem's exact language rather than free improvisation.
materials: Used paper bags with a base (one per student)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.41): revisit poem comprehension through a class recitation and discussion.
Let us think — B (p.41): draw together play experiences and poem content in a shared oral reflection.

time_bands.activity: Choral recitation of the full poem (pp.39–40): the class recites all three stanzas together, adding body actions for each action verb. Teacher leads the first run-through, then a student volunteer leads a second.

Whole-class discussion drawing on the poem's content: teacher asks one question per stanza — 'What did the child do with the ball?', 'How did the kite move?', 'Who did the child play with in the last stanza?' Students answer in complete sentences, connecting back to the poem's language.

Open oral reflection: students share which activity from the poem — ball-play, kite-flying, or playing with friends — they like most and why, using at least one 'and'-linked word pair from the chapter (e.g. 'I run and skip with my friends'). Teacher invites three to four students to speak.

Brief closing chant: the class recites the poem's repeating refrain — 'Out in the garden, / Each fine day. / I like to play.' — together as a whole-chapter send-off. Teacher celebrates effort across the poem study.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the ball, kite, and friends stanzas of the poem alongside the action-verb pairs and outdoor-play discussion the chapter explored. Where students struggle to recall a specific action verb, point them to the relevant stanza in the textbook rather than supplying the word yourself.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 39 beginning "I bounce my ball". Which of the following best describes what the child does with the ball in the poem?

options.label: A
options.text: The child bounces, throws, and catches the ball.

options.label: B
options.text: The child kicks, rolls, and spins the ball.

options.label: C
options.text: The child runs, skips, and swings the ball.

options.label: D
options.text: The child tugs, pulls, and flies the ball.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be drawing on general ball-game knowledge rather than the poem's specific verbs.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the kite-action verbs with the ball-action verbs — both appear in the poem but in different stanzas.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has taken the friends-stanza action verbs and applied them to the ball stanza.

items.item_stem: The poem names three things the child plays with in the garden. Look at the poem on pages 39–40 and write one sentence saying what the child does with the kite.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The child tugs, pulls, and flies the kite in the garden.

items.item_stem: The child in the poem plays in a garden. Look at the pictures of games on Textbook page 41. Decide whether each statement below is true or false.

options.text: Seven stones is a game played alone without any friends.
The picture on page 41 shows children pulling a rope in a tug-of-war.
The tin telephone picture shows two children using cans connected by a string.
The yo-yo picture shows a girl throwing a ball into the air.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: the tug-of-war illustration shows two teams pulling a rope. 2 — False: the yo-yo picture shows a boy spinning a yo-yo, not a ball being thrown. 3 — True: the tin telephone shows two children with cans joined by a string. 4 — False: seven stones is played with a group of children.

items.item_stem: The child in the poem plays outside with friends and says 'We run and skip, We jump and sway.' Talk about a game you love to play outside: where you play it, what you do, and one thing you must be careful about.

expected_elements: Names a specific outdoor game or play space.
Describes at least one action done in the game.
Mentions one safety point while playing.

items.item_stem: Look at the steps for making the paper bag puppet on Textbook page 43. Match each step number in Column A with the correct action in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A — Step | Column B — Action |
|---|---|
| Step 1 | Draw the upper lip on the line of the flap. |
| Step 2 | Slide your hand into the bag. |
| Step 3 | Fold the base of the bag upward. |
| Step 4 | Take a used paper bag with a base. |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Step 1 — c (Take a used paper bag with a base); Step 2 — c (Fold the base upward); Step 3 — a (Draw the upper lip on the line of the flap); Step 4 — b (Slide your hand into the bag). Short form: Step 1-d, Step 2-c, Step 3-a, Step 4-b.

answer_key.right: Take a used paper bag with a base.
Fold the base of the bag upward.
Draw the upper lip on the line of the flap.
Slide your hand into the bag.
